problem: Online RL for real-world robot navigation needs far too much trial-and-error or a high-fidelity sim-to-real pipeline. Imitation learning needs new reward-specific demonstrations for every new preference. Flat offline RL policies fail on long-horizon goals: IQL could not reach goals beyond about 20 m / 80 steps from first-person images.
motivation: Real navigation should often maximize a user utility (stay on grass, stay in sunlight, stay on pavement), not only reach the goal. An existing uncurated dataset can be relabeled post hoc with any reward and reused without collecting new data. Offline value functions are accurate only over short horizons, so they should be composed with planning over a topological 'mental map' to reach distant goals.
key_idea: Learn a goal-conditioned, reward-specific value function and policy with offline Implicit Q-Learning on relabeled prior robot data, use -V as edge cost in an image/GPS topological graph of the environment, and run Dijkstra to find a reward-maximizing path whose subgoals the learned policy executes.
insight: Flat reactive policies (BC, filtered BC, IQL) can encode reward preferences but degrade sharply with distance and 'bee-line' into obstacles. On the grassy task they reach 0/5 hard (150-500 m) goals, while adding the graph restores long-range success. The Q-learned value, not reward filtering, is what makes the graph path respect the utility: Filtered BC + Graph and ViNG match ReViND's easy/medium success, but on hard goals reach only 3/5 with grass utility 0.19 / 0.14, versus ReViND's 4/5 with 0.78. Proposition 3.1 justifies the design: with optimal short-horizon values, a dense graph and a deterministic MDP with γ=1, the min-cost path under edge weights -V* recovers the optimal long-horizon path.
method: Reward relabeling: the same 30 h offline dataset is relabeled with R_dist (-1 per step, 0 at goal) or with utility bonuses such as R_grass / R_sun = -1 + 0.75*1{grass/sun}. Labels come from HSV thresholding of the bottom-center image crop, manual labels (on-sidewalk), or a learned image reward classifier trained on a few manual labels (grassy, on-pavement).

Goal relabeling: goals are future states from the same trajectory, sampled 10-70 steps ahead (trajectories are about 80 steps); in practice the goal is only the relative GPS coordinate of the goal state.

Offline IQL training: Q(s,a,g) is regressed to r + γV(s',g), and V is trained with an expectile loss (τ=0.9) to approximate an in-distribution max without querying out-of-distribution actions. The policy is extracted by advantage weighting (policy weight 0.1, γ=0.99). Networks: IMPALA encoder on 64x48 RGB -> 50-d tanh/LayerNorm feature, concatenated with a 3-d goal, then 256-256 MLP heads for π (10-d output), Q and V.

Topological graph construction: nodes are sub-sampled images+GPS (10-30 m apart) from a prior teleoperated drive in the test environment; this data is not used for fine-tuning. Edges are added if timestamps are close (ε=1 s; the text also says <2 s), or if the learned distance -V < τ (50 steps, about 12 m) and GPS distance < η (100 m), which filters out wormholes. Edge weight is -V(n_i, relative goal), followed by a transitive reduction.

Deployment: the current observation and the goal are inserted as nodes, Dijkstra finds the min-cost (reward-maximizing) path, and the IQL policy drives toward the relative GPS vector of the first waypoint for H steps before replanning, all on-board a Jetson TX2.

setting.backbone: IMPALA CNN encoder + MLP policy/Q/value heads (trained from scratch with offline IQL)
setting.training_data: 30 hours of publicly available real-robot trajectories from randomized data collection in an office park (RECON dataset, Shah et al. 2021), relabeled post hoc with goals and reward labels (distance, grass, sun, pavement); no new data collection or fine-tuning
setting.observation: forward-facing 170° FOV monocular RGB (downsampled to 64x48) + unfiltered GPS; goal as relative GPS coordinate
setting.action_space: continuous 2D steering and throttle commands (policy outputs a 10-d action; baselines described as commanding future waypoints)
setting.privileged: prior teleoperated traversal of the test environment used to build the topological graph (pre-exploration); GPS localization

numbers_note: Real-world only, very small sample: 5 trials per difficulty bin. Success is printed as fractions (e.g. '5/5') and kept verbatim as strings. Table 1 SPL was printed as 0-1 values and converted to 0-100; E R_grass / E R_sun are normalized rewards and left as printed. The main text says five suburban test environments, while the appendix says 15 environments. The graph timestamp threshold is given as both <2 s and ε = 1 s. The reward trade-off sensitivity results (Fig. 5) appear only in a figure.
results: On the grassy task, ReViND matches graph-based baselines on easy/medium goals (5/5, 4/5) and beats them on hard 150-500 m goals: 4/5 success versus 3/5 for ViNG and Filtered BC + Graph. It also collects far more grass: hard-goal utility 0.78 versus 0.14 (ViNG) and 0.19 (fBC + Graph). The flat BC, fBC and IQL policies get 0/5 on hard goals. On the sunny task ReViND reaches 5/5, 3/5 and 4/5 success with the highest medium/hard sun utility (0.75 / 0.74 versus ViNG's 0.58 / 0.63). Changing only the reward changes behavior as intended: SPL 0.87 with R_grass 0.16 for R_dist; 0.84 with R_grass 0.86 for R_grass; 0.64 with R_sun 0.68 for R_sun.
limitations: All training data must be labeled with each reward, and the reward must stay valid across environments ('grassy' and 'sunny' vary by place and season). Behavior is bounded by what the offline data contains; e.g. it cannot learn off-road driving from road-only data.
Requires a prior traversal of the test environment to build the topological graph; exploration of unseen environments is left to future work. GPS is needed for edge filtering and goal specification.
Evaluation is small-scale and real-world only (5 trials per difficulty), in environments visually similar to the training data, with no standard benchmark.
